inbox.content: Polar bears (Ursus maritimus) depend on sea ice as a platform for hunting seals. Arctic sea ice has declined in extent and thickness over the satellite era as the Arctic has warmed about twice as fast as the global mean (Arctic amplification). The IUCN and Arctic scientists treat loss of sea-ice hunting habitat as the primary long-term threat to the species. Some subpopulations have been relatively stable or better counted in recent surveys, which deniers sometimes quote as 'polar bears are fine.' That snapshot does not cancel the physical dependence on ice or projections of increased fasting and reduced cub survival as ice-free seasons lengthen, especially in southern parts of the range. Polar-bear numbers are not a single global census with low error; management units differ. Conservation hunting quotas and pollution are additional pressures, but they do not make sea-ice loss irrelevant. There is no scientific basis for the claim that polar bears are thriving because of chemtrails or that global warming is a hoax because one subpopulation increased.

history.contentIn: The Stratospheric Controlled Perturbation Experiment (SCoPEx) was a scientific initiative by Harvard University aimed at examining the behavior of small aerosol particles within the stratosphere, with particular attention to their potential impacts on ozone and ecosystems. Led by principal investigator Frank Keutsch and collaborators, the project was introduced publicly in 2017, emphasizing its focus on enhancing computer models to assess the risks and benefits associated with solar geoengineering, rather than implementing immediate geoengineering solutions. The experiment proposed using a scientific balloon gondola flying at approximately 20 km altitude to release a minimal quantity of material—between 100 grams and 2 kilograms of calcium carbonate—into a carefully controlled volume for analysis. A planned 2021 platform test in Sweden was ultimately canceled to prioritize societal engagement, confirming that no particles would be released. In March 2024, Harvard announced the discontinuation of SCoPEx, with intentions to redirect the platform towards unrelated stratospheric research, thereby highlighting the need for caution and thorough ecological consideration in any future aerosol studies.

Polar bears (Ursus maritimus) depend on sea ice as a platform for hunting seals. Arctic sea ice has declined in extent and thickness over the satellite era as the Arctic has warmed about twice as fast as the global mean (Arctic amplification). The IUCN and Arctic scientists treat loss of sea-ice hunting habitat as the primary long-term threat to the species. Some subpopulations have been relatively stable or better counted in recent surveys, which deniers sometimes quote as 'polar bears are fine.' That snapshot does not cancel the physical dependence on ice or projections of increased fasting and reduced cub survival as ice-free seasons lengthen, especially in southern parts of the range. Polar-bear numbers are not a single global census with low error; management units differ. Conservation hunting quotas and pollution are additional pressures, but they do not make sea-ice loss irrelevant. There is no scientific basis for the claim that polar bears are thriving because of chemtrails or that global warming is a hoax because one subpopulation increased.
